claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has a ductile matrix containing discrete intermetallic or second phases.
Dissimilar phases in the eutectic microstructure can exhibit different electrochemical potentials and undergo interphase galvanic corrosion.
An oxide film forms on the alloy surface during friction and wear and contributes to wear resistance.
Rupture of the oxide film during friction promotes adhesive and abrasive wear.
Sliding wear preferentially removes protective oxide films at phase boundaries.
Wear-induced film removal exposes fresh surfaces of the dissimilar phases.
Potential differences between the exposed phases establish galvanic cells.
The galvanic cells preferentially corrode the less noble phase.
Galvanic attack is localized at phase boundaries.
Galvanic corrosion further destabilizes the oxide film and thereby enhances subsequent wear.
Wear-induced depassivation and interphase galvanic corrosion form a positive feedback loop that amplifies both wear and corrosion.
Under simultaneous elevated-temperature sliding and corrosive exposure, the multiphase eutectic alloy will have a higher total degradation rate than a homogeneous single-phase baseline.
Combined exposure will increase wear-related material loss relative to the baseline.
Combined exposure will produce higher corrosion current density and more pit formation at phase boundaries relative to the baseline.
The proposed synergy requires elevated temperature, active sliding, and a corrosive medium, and may be absent at lower temperature or under static conditions.
A lack of statistically significant increases in both wear and corrosion in the multiphase alloy would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The design includes only simultaneous wear-corrosion tests of multiphase and single-phase samples, but the falsification rule requires comparison with the sum of degradation measured under the individual wear and corrosion modes. Those isolated-mode arms are absent from the design.

The predicted outcome treats higher total degradation, higher wear, and higher corrosion as separate expectations, whereas the falsification rule presents total degradation exceeding the sum of individual modes as equivalent to statistically significant increases in both wear and corrosion. These criteria are not logically equivalent.

The baseline field allows either a single-phase alloy or isolated wear/corrosion tests at lower temperature, while the experiment specifies only a single-phase microstructural control under simultaneous exposure. This makes the stated baseline non-unique and changes more than one variable in the lower-temperature alternative.
